design_detail: Critical narrative review of human studies on methamphetamine and cognition: 16 acute laboratory dosing studies (Table 1), PET studies (Table 2), MRI/fMRI/DTI studies (Table 3) and neuropsychological battery studies (Table 4), each tabulated with the reviewers' caveats. Includes the reviewers' own comparisons of published group means against normative data for two studies.
can_establish: Where specific primary studies over-interpret their data (group differences described as dysfunction, cognition untested in controls, normative comparisons absent, education gaps), each point checkable against the primary paper; and what controlled laboratory dosing studies showed for acute effects.
cannot_establish: That the literature as a whole shows no cognitive effect of methamphetamine: there is no systematic search, no stated inclusion criteria beyond excluding HIV-positive samples, no risk-of-bias assessment and no pooled estimate, so the selection of studies cannot be checked for completeness.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Studies tabulated: 16 acute laboratory studies (Table 1, pp. 590–591), 16 PET studies (Table 2, pp. 593–595), 13 MRI/fMRI/DTI studies (Table 3, pp. 599–601), 7 neuropsychological battery studies (Table 4, pp. 603–604).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated, except that studies including HIV-positive participants were excluded (p. 592). No databases, search terms or dates are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Unknown completeness; the reviewers' own laboratory authored or co-authored 7 of the 16 acute studies in Table 1 (Comer 2001; Hart 2001, 2002, 2008; Kirkpatrick 2008 and in press; Marrone 2010, per the reference list, pp. 605–607).

exposure.polysubstance: The review notes that in most imaging studies users reported extensive other drug use while controls reported little, making methamphetamine-specific effects hard to isolate (pp. 597–598).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Acute studies: oral, intranasal or intravenous doses up to 50 mg/70 kg (intranasal) or 30 mg (intravenous), single administrations, given to people with limited stimulant experience or with methamphetamine use disorder (pp. 589–592; Table 1). Reported here as study conditions.

comparison.controls: Acute studies: placebo within participant. Chronic studies: non-using controls.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review's central point for chronic studies: single-time-point comparisons cannot exclude pre-existing differences (e.g. p. 598).

outcomes.instruments: As in the primary studies; the review classifies findings by cognitive domain.
outcomes.validity_norms: The reviewers compared published group means with normative data for McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) (pp. 596, 602) but do not report which norms, cut-offs or values were used.
outcomes.operationalization: Distinguishes two meanings of impairment: a statistically significant group difference, and a loss of function outside the normal range with clinical significance (p. 596).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Narrative and tabulated counts of significant and non-significant findings by domain.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable: no search or selection method reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Controlled single-dose laboratory studies found no cognitive disruption and some improvement at the doses tested; chronic-use studies found statistically significant user–control differences on a minority of measures, frequently without normative comparison, education matching or control of other drug use; several primary papers draw causal or clinical conclusions their designs cannot support.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion states that the widely publicized methamphetamine–cognitive impairment link is not supported by research evidence (p. 605) and that concerns about cognitive deficits compromising engagement in cognitive-behavioural treatment are not warranted (p. 605). The review's own material shows the link is not established, not that it is refuted: significant differences exist on some measures, and individual-level impairment in a minority of users is documented in one study it discusses (Kalechstein et al., 2003, p. 602). The normative re-analyses that carry much of the argument are not reproducible as reported.

timeline.event: Response review argues the preponderance of evidence supports mild cognitive decline in at least some users and rejects a categorical normal/impaired reading
Meta-analysis of 44 studies finds moderate average deficits with strong evidence of publication bias
Meta-analysis restricted to abstinent samples finds small-to-moderate differences and calls strong statements premature
Meta-analysis of 68 newer studies: medium-to-large average differences, prediction intervals including zero, GRADE very low

replication.where_it_stands: The review's specific criticisms of primary studies are checkable and, for the four Volkow-group imaging papers, confirmed on reading (cognition tested in users only, no education data). Its overall conclusion remains contested; see the debate on cognition.

funding.funder: Open Society Foundation and National Institute on Drug Abuse grants DA-03746 and DA-019559 (p. 605).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 605).
funding.affiliations_note: The first author's laboratory produced 7 of the 16 acute studies reviewed in Table 1. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review applying a normative (demographically adjusted) impairment criterion to individual-level data from all user–control studies, alongside group differences; and prospective cohorts with pre-use cognitive baselines.

domains.note: No databases, terms or dates reported.

domains.domain: Inclusion criteria and list of excluded studies
domains.note: Only the HIV exclusion is stated (p. 592).

domains.domain: Risk of bias assessed in included studies
domains.note: No formal tool, but each study's caveats are tabulated (Tables 1–4).

domains.domain: Risk of bias considered when interpreting results
domains.note: The interpretation is built on study limitations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged as a systematic summary, confidence is critically low because the search and selection are not reported. It does not claim to be systematic; its value is as a set of specific, checkable critiques of individual studies, which this encyclopedia verifies against each primary paper before relying on them.

key_findings.finding: In 16 controlled acute dosing studies, single doses of methamphetamine (up to 50 mg/70 kg intranasal or 30 mg intravenous in the studies tested) produced no cognitive disruption and improved performance in some domains (visuospatial perception, sustained attention, response speed); repeated or binge dosing was not tested.
key_findings.locator: Review of the Acute Effects; Table 1 (pp. 590–591)

key_findings.finding: Animal neurotoxicity regimens typically give large bolus doses to drug-naive animals; prior escalating doses can prevent the neurotoxic effects of a later binge (Segal et al., 2003; O'Neil et al., 2006; Belcher et al., 2008).
In McCann et al. (1998), DAT binding in users overlapped considerably with controls, and all users reported other illicit drug use.

Johanson et al. (2006): DAT and VMAT2 binding 10–16% lower in 16 abstinent users than 18 controls; users differed on a minority of tests and stayed within the normal range for age and education; no relation between imaging and cognition.

The reviewers compared the mean scores of users in McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) with published norms and found none outside the normal range; Simon et al. (2010) did not replicate the 2002 group differences.
key_findings.note: Norms, cut-offs and values used are not reported.

key_findings.finding: The term impairment is used both for a statistically significant group difference and for clinically meaningful loss of function; studies often report the first and discuss it as the second.
key_findings.locator: Main text, last paragraph before 'PET studies investigating brain metabolism'

key_findings.finding: Thompson et al. (2004) reported smaller hippocampal (7.8%) and cingulate (11.3%) grey matter in users, but did not compare memory performance between groups, scanned once, and controls had more schooling (15.2 vs 12.8 years).
Kalechstein et al. (2003): about 7 of 27 users vs 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD normative impairment criterion in at least one domain.
The four Volkow-group PET papers are tabulated as reporting no education data and no cognitive comparison with controls.
key_findings.note: The review letters these papers differently: its 2001a is the metabolism paper, 2001b the DAT paper, 2001d the recovery paper.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: acute doses improve some cognitive functions; chronic-use differences are on a minority of measures and mostly within the normal range; brain differences are frequently over-interpreted as pathology.

reporting_issues.issue: The normative re-analyses of McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) are described in one sentence each, without the norms, cut-offs or numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: A central plank of the argument cannot be reproduced from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: A group mean within the normal range does not show that individuals are within it; the review's own discussion of Kalechstein et al. (2003) shows a minority meeting an impairment criterion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The normative test answers 'is the average user impaired?', not 'are some users impaired?'.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's lettering of the 2001 Volkow papers differs from their citation elsewhere; the Wang et al. (2004) entry omits the Symbol Digit correlation reported in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; readers should match by title.
